section_summary: This section documents U.S. State Department efforts between November 1935 and October 1938 to protect the practice rights of American attorneys residing in Japan—specifically William B. Spencer in Yokohama, William J. Sebald in Kobe, and C. C. Smith in Tokyo—under Japan's Lawyers' Law of 1933 (Law No. 53), which took effect in April 1936 and restricted legal practice to Japanese subjects except where foreign reciprocity was certified. To satisfy the Japanese Ministry of Justice, the State Department coordinated with bar and judicial authorities in the District of Columbia and Maryland to obtain authenticated certificates demonstrating that Japanese lawyers in those jurisdictions were permitted to advise their countrymen on Japanese and foreign law without formal admission to the bar. These authenticated credentials were transmitted through diplomatic instructions and urgent telegraphic instructions to Ambassador Joseph C. Grew in Tokyo for formal delivery to the Japanese Government.

subfiles.about: Diplomatic despatch transmitting and analyzing English translations of Japan's Lawyers' Law of 1933 and related legislation restricting legal practice to Japanese subjects unless reciprocity is established.
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Chargé d'Affaires ad interim Edwin L. Neville reports on the newly enacted Lawyers' Law of Japan (Law No. 53 of 1933), scheduled to take effect on April 1, 1936. He notes that Articles 2 and 6 restrict the practice of law to Japanese subjects unless the Minister of Justice grants permission to foreign lawyers upon assurance of reciprocity. Neville reports having conferred with the three American lawyers currently in Japan, who practice strictly as consultants outside Japanese courts, and suggests that pending regulations might accommodate consulting work on a reciprocal basis. The despatch transmits complete English translations of Law No. 53, establishing qualifications, bar associations, rights and duties, and disciplinary courts, as well as Law No. 54 of 1933 regarding the control of handling legal affairs.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1559: Lawyers' Law of Japan (Law No. 53 of the Year 1933)

subfiles.about: Letter from an American lawyer in Yokohama requesting State Department assistance to secure an official reciprocity certificate from the District of Columbia to satisfy the Japanese Department of Justice.
subfiles.from: William B. Spencer, Attorney-at-Law and Patent Attorney, Yokohama, Japan
subfiles.summary: William B. Spencer, an American attorney and patent attorney practicing in Yokohama, writes to the Secretary of State on behalf of himself, C. C. Smith of Tokyo, and William J. Sebald of Kobe regarding their applications for permits under Article 6 of Japan's Lawyers' Law of 1933. Spencer explains that although he submitted a letter dated February 19, 1936 from John Paul Earnest, Chairman of the Committee on Admissions and Grievances of the District of Columbia Bar, the Japanese Department of Justice required certification by a recognized U.S. government department or ambassador, similar to a certificate obtained by British barrister John Gadsby. Emphasizing that American attorneys represent major U.S. commercial interests in Japan—such as Universal Pictures, Carnation, IBM, and Dollar Steamship Line—Spencer asks the State Department to certify that Japanese lawyers may advise their countrymen in the District of Columbia without appearing in court. The letter is accompanied by copies of the Earnest letter and the British certificate, along with duplicate carbon copies.
subfiles.title: Letter from William B. Spencer Regarding Permission to Practice Law in Japan Under the Lawyers' Law of 1933
subfiles.to: Secretary of State, Washington (Attention: Mr. Ward, Legal Department)

subfiles.title: Letter from William B. Spencer Providing Temporary Address in Washington, D.C.

subfiles.about: State Department letter informing William B. Spencer that an authenticated chain of certificates establishing reciprocity in the District of Columbia has been forwarded to Tokyo.
subfiles.from: Green H. Hackworth, Legal Adviser (For the Secretary of State)
subfiles.summary: Hackworth tells Spencer the D.C. Committee on Admissions' certification chain, authenticated by the Chief Justice, Attorney General and State, went to Ambassador Grew for Japan's Justice Department to issue his practice permit.
subfiles.title: Letter from Legal Adviser Green H. Hackworth to William B. Spencer

subfiles.about: Diplomatic instruction transmitting authenticated District of Columbia credentials to Ambassador Joseph C. Grew in Tokyo to secure William B. Spencer's law practice permit.
subfiles.from: R. Walton Moore (For the Secretary of State)
subfiles.summary: Instruction No. 1530 asks Grew to help American attorney William Spencer obtain a permit under Japan's 1933 Lawyers' Law, transmitting his petition, the Earnest statement and authentications.
subfiles.title: Instruction No. 1530 to Ambassador Joseph C. Grew Regarding William B. Spencer's Practice of Law in Japan
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
